meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'for nothing, in vain', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You're wasting your time.
I came for nothing.

examples.text: Вы зря теряете время. Шпионить для вас я не буду.
examples.trans: You're wasting your time. I'm not going to spy for you.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.
And does the governor support you?

examples.text: Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'with', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Share with everyone.
I'm with Dad.
Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'oneself', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I feel good.
He only thinks about himself.

examples.text: А с Пашей я снова чувствую себя женщиной.
examples.trans: And with Pasha I feel like a woman again.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'вести'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to bring, lead'.

examples.trans: You will bring the child in the morning.

examples.text: Нужно срочно привести его в человеческий вид!
examples.trans: He must urgently be brought into a presentable state!

examples.text: Они привели нового шеф-повара прямо из Индии.
examples.trans: They brought a new chef straight from India.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'yes, indeed', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh yeah?
Yes, it's me.
Oh yeah? When?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian expressive spoken interjection meaning 'hello, hey', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Right, quiet, everyone! Hello?

examples.text: Алло, Танечка! В свои годы это нормально.
examples.trans: Hello, Tanechka! At my age that's normal.
Hello, Ilyusha, hi. It's Anikeev.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you.
And where's the toy car?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'we', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We've done a lot.
Our toilet is dirty.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything, all; that's it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
That's it, bye!

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to know'.

examples.trans: I don't know.
As you all know...

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'how; as', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How was it in Hungary?
As you all know...
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'знать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to recognise; to find out', paired with 'узнавать'.

examples.trans: Did you recognise me?
I'll find out where he is.
You recognised me. Thanks for seeing me.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'shop, store' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Let's go to the shop.
The shop is already closed.
What to do? Let's go to the shop.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto; for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('other, another, different').

examples.trans: Could we go somewhere else?
That's a different building.

examples.text: Послушайте, а можно в другое место? Здесь плохо пахнет.
examples.trans: Listen, could we go somewhere else? It smells bad in here.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'торона'). Common feminine noun meaning 'side' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: On the other hand, it's interesting.
The shop is on that side.

examples.text: Бред какой-то. Но, с другой стороны, чем я рискую?
examples.trans: What nonsense. But on the other hand, what have I got to lose?

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'лица'). Common feminine noun meaning 'street; outside' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: There are reporters out on the street!
It is cold outside.

examples.text: Там на улице журналисты! Они меня ждут!
examples.trans: There are reporters out on the street! They're waiting for me!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'here is; (emphasis) that's', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: All right, here you go. There, look.
There, look.
You'll see!

справа.gloss: on the right, to the right

meanings.en: on the right, to the right
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'права').

examples.trans: There to the right of the door!
The shop is located to the right of the entrance.

examples.text: Как не нашла? Послушай, в чёрном шкафу посмотри. Там справа от двери!
examples.trans: What do you mean you didn't find it? Listen, look in the black cabinet. There to the right of the door!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for; behind', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Thank you for your trust!
Thanks for the present.
What for?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'corner' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: He's sitting in the corner.
The café is on the corner.
Why are you sitting in the corner?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'trash bin, urn' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Да выбрось её скорее в урну.
examples.trans: Just throw it out quickly into the trash bin.

examples.text: Всё по правилам, как рыцарский турнир.
examples.trans: All by the rules, like a knights' tournament.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'ложить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to put, to lay down', paired with 'класть'.

examples.text: В гроб с собой икру не положишь!
examples.trans: You can't put caviar in your coffin to take with you!
Put the keys on the table.

examples.text: А вот сюда я её и положу! Отличный подарок будет!
examples.trans: Right here is where I will put it! It will be an excellent gift!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'there, thither', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я знаю! Хочешь, сейчас и тебя туда увезут?
examples.trans: I know! Do you want them to take you there too right now?
They put bad meat in there for you.
Let's go there together.

meanings.note: Common Russian noun meaning 'money' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I have no money.
The money is on the table.
Gum? I didn't have enough money.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.
Dad and Mum.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'ходить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to leave, to go away', paired with 'уйти'.

examples.trans: I'm going home.
You are. Go away.
I'm leaving.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Это хорошо, что готово. А то мы уже начали беспокоиться.
examples.trans: It's good that it's ready. We were starting to worry.

examples.text: А если я не скажу, то что? Ты мне ухо отрежешь?
examples.trans: And if I don't tell you, then what? Will you cut my ear off?

examples.text: А если я не скажу, то что?
examples.trans: And if I don't tell you, then what?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
I'm doing my homework.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'already', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.
Dad is already home.
I'm already home.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'work, job' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I'm going to work.
There's a lot of work.
I'm at work.

опаздывать.gloss: to be running late, to be late

meanings.en: to be running late, to be late
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be running late, to be late', paired with 'опоздать'.

examples.trans: Listen, I really am running late.
Don't be late for the train!

examples.text: Ладно, Артурик. Послушай, я правда опаздываю.
examples.trans: All right, Arturik. Listen, I really am running late.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian cardinal or ordinal numeral meaning 'one', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Give me just one.
I have one brother.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'well; come on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh, come on, Dad!
Well?

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: I was only looking.
Just one.
I was only looking!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for the sake of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: It's all for us.
I'll do anything for you.
Work, work. It's all for us.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.trans: They called from the Italian restaurant.
In the evening they went to a restaurant.

examples.text: Кстати, звонили из итальянского ресторана. Дарят папе романтический ужин на двоих.
examples.trans: By the way, they called from the Italian restaurant. They're giving Dad a romantic dinner for two.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'matter; thing to do' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I have a lot to do.
How are things?

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's what you said.
That house is old.
Well, the thing you said.
